meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Always do sober what you said you'd do drunk. That will teach you to keep your mouth shut'?
meta.ogDescription: Traced to a private Hemingway letter reported in Forbes in 1961 and recalled in Scribner's 1990 memoir. Credible, but no primary source pins the exact wording.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: Hemingway is widely and credibly credited with this line, which is said to come from a private letter of “rules for life” he sent to his publisher Charles Scribner Jr. in the 1950s. But that letter has never been published, the evidence is second-hand — Malcolm Forbes printed it in 1961, Scribner recalled it in a 1990 memoir — and the two accounts word it differently, so no primary source pins this exact phrasing.

source.excerpt: Always do sober what you said you’d do drunk. That will teach you to keep your mouth shut.
trail: September 1961 — the first printing. Malcolm S. Forbes wrote in Forbes that Hemingway closed a letter to Charles Scribner with a list of rules, the first being “Always do sober what you said you’d do drunk: That will teach you to keep your mouth shut.” Forbes never explained how he saw a private letter — Quote Investigator lays out the chronology ↗.

1962–1964 — the wording drifts. QI records reprints in the Atlantic Coast Line News and The Berkshire Eagle, a “big mouth shut” variant in 1963 newspapers, and a further rephrasing in Bennett Cerf’s syndicated column of 25 April 1964 — all documented in QI’s chronology ↗.

1990 — the recipient speaks. Charles Scribner Jr. quoted the rule in his memoir In the Company of Writers: A Life in Publishing, page 64. The book was published in New York by Charles Scribner’s Sons in 1990 — catalogue record at the Internet Archive ↗. Wikiquote cites this page in its sourced Hemingway section ↗.

Still not in the scholarly edition. The Cambridge edition of Hemingway’s letters — roughly 7,000 letters, about 85 percent previously unpublished, in a projected seventeen volumes — had reached June 1936 with Volume 6 in May 2024, per the Hemingway Letters Project ↗. The 1950s Scribner letter is not yet in print there.
source.excerptNote: No fuller original context exists in print. Quote Investigator records the September 1961 Forbes printing with a colon — “…do drunk: That will teach you to keep your mouth shut” — while Charles Scribner Jr.’s own 1990 memoir gives “…what you said you’d do when you were drunk. That will teach you to keep your mouth shut!”

source.rightsNote: This is not a pre-1931 published work. The line is said to come from a private Hemingway letter of the 1950s whose earliest documented printing is Forbes in September 1961, and the fullest citable version appears in a memoir published in 1990. Both are comfortably inside US copyright, and an author’s unpublished letters remain the property of the estate — so treat this as in-copyright, not public domain.

author.name: Ernest Hemingway
author.heading: The man on the letterhead
author.metaLine: 1899–1961 · American novelist, short-story writer and journalist
author.bio: Ernest Hemingway wrote The Sun Also Rises, A Farewell to Arms and The Old Man and the Sea, and spent his whole career with one publisher, Charles Scribner’s Sons. He won the Pulitzer Prize in 1953 and the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1954. His reputation as a heroic drinker is exactly why lines like this one stick to his name so easily — and why they deserve checking.

misattribution.heading: What gets garbled
misattribution.intro: Nobody serious credits this line to the wrong person — the problem is the words themselves. Because the underlying letter has never been printed, every version in circulation is somebody’s memory of it, and they differ.

items.who: “…what you said you’d do when you were drunk”
items.why: This longer phrasing is the one Charles Scribner Jr. gave in his own 1990 memoir In the Company of Writers, page 64, and repeated in a 1993 book. Since Scribner was the man who received the letter, his version has a real claim — but Quote Investigator says plainly that it is uncertain which version is more accurate ↗.

An extra word crept in almost immediately. QI records the “big mouth” form in 1963 newspapers including The Salinas Californian and The Pensacola News ↗, and a further rephrasing in Bennett Cerf’s syndicated column of 25 April 1964.

items.who: Shared with no source at all
items.why: The version most people meet online carries Hemingway’s name and nothing else. Goodreads hosts it with thousands of likes and no book cited ↗, noting that its quotes are community-added and not verified.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest position: Quote Investigator concludes there is substantive evidence Hemingway wrote a comment of this type ↗ to Charles Scribner in the 1950s — but the letter is unpublished, so the exact sentence is a reconstruction, not a transcription.

context.heading: Why this one is hard to nail down
lead: Charles Scribner Jr. took over Charles Scribner’s Sons in 1952, on the death of his father. Hemingway — a Scribner author since The Sun Also Rises in 1926, and by then the firm’s most famous name — wrote the new boss a long personal letter that, according to everyone who has described it, closed with a short list of rules for living. This was the first rule.

The trouble is that nobody has ever printed the letter. What survives is two people’s memory of it: Malcolm Forbes, who published a version in Forbes in September 1961 without ever explaining how he came by a private letter, and Scribner himself, who quoted a slightly different version in his 1990 memoir. Both make Hemingway the author. Neither settles the words.
context.detailsSummary: Why the definitive edition can’t help yet
detailsBody: The Hemingway Letters Project is producing a scholarly edition of roughly 7,000 letters, about 85 percent of them never before published, in a projected seventeen volumes from Cambridge University Press. As of Volume 6, published in May 2024, the edition covers correspondence through June 1936.

A 1950s letter to Charles Scribner Jr. therefore falls well beyond the published run. Until the edition reaches the 1950s — or the letter itself surfaces in the Scribner archive — the wording of this line rests on the recollections of two men, printed twenty-nine years apart, that do not quite match.
context.pull: “Always do sober what you said you’d do when you were drunk” — the version Charles Scribner Jr. himself remembered.
